title: Practice: choosing and misleading graphs
intro: Nine questions on picking the right graph and seeing through the wrong ones.

questions.prompt: Match each set of data to the most appropriate graph.

left.text: Times taken to travel to school, grouped
Average temperature each month of the year

hints: Proportions of a whole → pie. Trend over time → line. Two variables → scatter.
questions.explanation: Categories → bar chart. Parts of a whole → pie chart. Grouped continuous → histogram. Change over time → line graph. A relationship → scatter graph.

questions.prompt: Hockey results for 30 matches. Find the pie chart angles.
Make the profits chart **misleading**: start the $y$-axis at 20 so that Year 3 looks 6 times as tall as Year 1.
questions.explanation: From 20, the bars are 2, 6 and 12 high, so Year 3 looks 6 times Year 1 — really it is only about 1.45 times.

questions.prompt: A company wants its profits to look like they are **growing fast**. Which tricks would do that?

options.text: Draw Year 3 with a dark colour and a thick border
Use 3D bars viewed from an angle
Show the profits as a pie chart

hints: Two of these would make the growth look *smaller* or hide it.
questions.explanation: Cutting the baseline, highlighting Year 3 and 3D effects all exaggerate. Stretching the axis makes growth look smaller, and a pie chart hides the trend altogether.

questions.prompt: A misleading graph must contain incorrect numbers.
hints: Re-read the lesson: what can be changed without changing the data?
questions.explanation: False. A graph can show completely correct data and still give a false impression through its axes, scale or style.

questions.prompt: In a pie chart of 100 dollars of spending, music gets $72^\circ$. How many dollars were spent on music?
A café's pictogram uses one cup for 20 soft drinks. Complete the table.
questions.explanation: Multiply the number of cups by 20: 60, 80, 50 and 100.

questions.prompt: Monthly highs: Dubai goes from 24 °C in January to 41 °C in July; London from 7 °C to 21 °C. Which is a sensible inference?

options.text: Both cities are hottest in the middle of the year, and Dubai is always much hotter
London is hotter than Dubai in winter
The temperature in both cities never changes

hints: An inference should follow from the evidence.
questions.explanation: Both peak in July/August and Dubai stays well above London all year. Option d predicts beyond the data, which the graph cannot support.

questions.prompt: A histogram of the heights of 1000 adults is symmetrical with a single peak in the middle. What is this shape called?
hints: It is also called a bell curve.
questions.explanation: A symmetrical bell shape is the normal distribution. If the peak were pushed to one side it would be skewed.
